title: Losartan and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Dizziness, Kidneys and HCTZ
excerpt: Can you drink on losartan? How alcohol and losartan both lower blood pressure, why losartan-HCTZ needs extra care, which hangover painkillers to avoid, and when to call a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on losartan? How alcohol and losartan lower blood pressure, why losartan-HCTZ needs extra care, and warning signs that need a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most people who take losartan can have an occasional drink, and there's no dangerous chemical reaction between the two. The real issue is that alcohol and losartan both lower your blood pressure, so together they can push it lower than you expect. That shows up as dizziness, light-headedness when you stand, and in some cases fainting. Over the longer term, regular heavy drinking pushes blood pressure back up and works against the very thing losartan is treating. If you take losartan with hydrochlorothiazide (the combination sold as Hyzaar and its generics), the dizziness risk is a bit higher, because the water pill adds its own blood-pressure-lowering effect and the official label specifically warns about alcohol.

**The quick rules:** Keep to light or moderate drinking, which US guidelines define as up to one drink a day for women and up to two for men. Have your first drink with food, sip water between drinks, and get up slowly from sitting or lying down. Don't skip your losartan dose to "make room" for drinking. Don't take ibuprofen or naproxen for a hangover headache without checking with your pharmacist first. And if a night of drinking leaves you vomiting or with diarrhea you can't keep up with, call your doctor or pharmacist about whether to pause your dose until you're keeping fluids down.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and your full medication list. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on losartan if** you also take a water pill, have kidney disease, have heart failure, have been told your potassium runs high, have diabetes, or have had dizzy spells or fainting since starting the medicine. **Get urgent care (call 911 in the US) if** you faint, have chest pain, a very slow or very irregular heartbeat, severe weakness, confusion, or trouble breathing, or if your lips, tongue, face, or throat swell.

## How Losartan Works, in Plain Words

Losartan (brand name Cozaar) belongs to a group of blood pressure medicines called **angiotensin II receptor blockers**, usually shortened to **ARBs**. Other members of the family include valsartan, irbesartan, olmesartan, candesartan, and telmisartan.

Your body makes a hormone called **angiotensin II** that tightens your blood vessels and tells your kidneys to hold on to salt and water. Both effects raise blood pressure. Losartan sits on the receptors that angiotensin II normally plugs into and blocks them. The result is that your blood vessels relax, your kidneys let go of a bit more salt and water, and your blood pressure comes down.

Doctors prescribe losartan for:

- **High blood pressure (hypertension)**, its most common use.
- **Kidney protection in people with type 2 diabetes** who have protein in their urine.
- **Lowering stroke risk** in some people with high blood pressure and a thickened heart muscle.
- **Heart failure**, in some cases, often when another medicine isn't tolerated (it's sometimes used off-label for this).

Losartan is taken once or twice a day, and it works steadily in the background. Your liver converts part of each dose into a more active form, and the blood-pressure-lowering effect lasts around the clock with regular dosing. That last point matters for drinking, because it means there's no "safe window" in the day when losartan isn't working.

## Why Losartan and Alcohol Can Be a Problem: The Real Mechanism

There's no toxic by-product and no liver clash here, unlike [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol). The interaction is about blood pressure and fluid balance, and it works on three time scales.

### 1. In the first few hours: two things lowering your blood pressure at once

Alcohol widens (dilates) blood vessels, especially in the skin, which is why some people get flushed and warm. In the hours right after drinking, that tends to lower blood pressure. Losartan is already relaxing your blood vessels. Put them together and the effects add up.

For most people on a stable dose, a drink or two produces nothing more than a mild drop they never notice. But the drop can be bigger if you:

- Drink several drinks quickly or on an empty stomach.
- Are dehydrated, hot, or have been exercising or sitting in a sauna or hot tub.
- Recently started losartan or had your dose increased.
- Also take a water pill or another blood pressure medicine.
- Are older, since the body's reflexes that catch a falling blood pressure get slower with age.

The classic symptom is **orthostatic (postural) hypotension**: a drop in blood pressure when you stand up. You stand from a bar stool or get out of bed to use the bathroom at night, and the room goes gray, your head swims, or your knees buckle. Most falls linked to this combination happen exactly then.

### 2. The next day: dehydration and your kidneys

Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to save water. That's why you pee more when you drink. A night of drinking, especially with vomiting or diarrhea, can leave you noticeably dry the next morning.

Losartan changes how your kidneys handle a low-fluid situation. Normally, when you're dehydrated, angiotensin II helps keep blood flowing through the kidney's filters. With that signal blocked, a kidney that's short on fluid has a harder time keeping its filtering rate up. In a healthy person after a normal night out, this rarely matters. But real dehydration (repeated vomiting, diarrhea, not drinking water for a day) is one of the known situations in which ARBs can contribute to a sudden drop in kidney function, called acute kidney injury.

This is why many health systems, including NHS services in the UK, give people on ARBs and ACE inhibitors "sick day" guidance: if you're losing fluids from vomiting, diarrhea, or fever and can't keep fluids down, contact your doctor or pharmacist about pausing the medicine until you're eating and drinking normally again. A rough hangover with vomiting falls into the same category. Don't stop the medicine on your own for longer than that without advice.

### 3. Over weeks and months: alcohol pushes blood pressure up

This is the part people miss. The short-term blood-pressure-lowering effect of alcohol doesn't last. After the first several hours, blood pressure tends to rebound, and regular drinking of more than moderate amounts is one of the best-established causes of high blood pressure. The American Heart Association and most hypertension guidelines list cutting back on alcohol as a standard lifestyle step for lowering blood pressure, and reviews of trials have found that people who drink heavily and cut back see their blood pressure fall.

So if you take losartan and drink heavily most days, you may be working against your own medicine. You may need a higher dose or a second drug to get the same control. For the full picture on this, see our guide to [alcohol and blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025).

## What the Official Label Says

The US prescribing information for losartan (Cozaar) does not list alcohol as a specific drug interaction. Its warnings focus on low blood pressure (especially in people who are low on fluid or salt), high potassium, changes in kidney function, and pregnancy. The general consumer advice you'll see from pharmacies and drug-information services is to limit alcohol because it can add to the blood-pressure-lowering effect and make dizziness more likely.

The combination pill is different. **Losartan with hydrochlorothiazide (Hyzaar)** contains a thiazide water pill, and the hydrochlorothiazide part of the label does list alcohol: alcohol (along with barbiturates and narcotic painkillers) may make orthostatic hypotension worse. In other words, the label specifically warns that drinking can make you more likely to feel faint when you stand up.

Two other label points are worth knowing because they connect to drinking habits:

- **NSAID painkillers** (ibuprofen, naproxen, high-dose aspirin) can blunt losartan's effect on blood pressure and, especially in people who are older, dehydrated, or have kidney problems, can harm kidney function.
- **Potassium**: losartan can raise potassium levels, so the label cautions against potassium supplements and potassium-containing salt substitutes unless a doctor has approved them.

## Can You Drink on Losartan? A Practical Answer

For a typical healthy adult on a stable dose with no kidney problems and no water pill, light to moderate drinking is generally considered acceptable, and many doctors say so directly. "Moderate" in the US Dietary Guidelines means **up to one standard drink a day for women and up to two for men**, on days you drink. A standard drink is about 12 oz of regular beer, 5 oz of wine, or 1.5 oz of 80-proof liquor.

Some people should be more careful, or should ask their doctor before drinking at all:

- People who take **losartan-HCTZ** or a separate water pill (furosemide, chlorthalidone, spironolactone, and others).
- People on **two or more blood pressure medicines**, such as losartan plus amlodipine or a beta blocker.
- People with **chronic kidney disease** or diabetic kidney disease, which is one of the main reasons losartan is prescribed.
- People with **heart failure**.
- People who've been told their **potassium is high**.
- **Older adults**, or anyone who has fallen or fainted.
- Anyone who has noticed dizziness since starting losartan.

If none of those apply, the practical approach is to drink less and slower than you might otherwise, eat with your drinks, and pay attention to how you feel the first few times. If one or two drinks reliably leave you dizzy on losartan, that's useful information to bring to your doctor, not something to push through.

## How Long After Taking Losartan Can You Drink?

There isn't a meaningful waiting period. Losartan is designed to keep your blood pressure lower all day and all night, so there's no point in the day when it has "worn off" and alcohol becomes safer. Spacing a drink a few hours from your pill won't change much.

What does help:

- **Keep taking your dose at the usual time.** Skipping it so you can drink is a bad trade. Your blood pressure may climb, and when you restart you can get a bigger drop than usual.
- **If you take losartan at night**, be extra careful about getting up to use the bathroom after drinking. That's the moment the combination is most likely to make you lightheaded.
- **If you've just started losartan or just had your dose raised**, consider holding off on alcohol for the first week or two, until you know how the medicine affects you.

## Losartan-HCTZ and Alcohol: Why the Combination Pill Needs More Care

Losartan-HCTZ combines losartan with hydrochlorothiazide, a thiazide diuretic (water pill). The diuretic lowers blood pressure partly by making you pass more salt and water. Add alcohol, which also makes you pee more, and you get a double push toward dehydration on top of the double push toward low blood pressure.

That's why people on the combination pill are more likely to feel dizzy after drinking, and why its label specifically mentions alcohol. A few extra points for this group:

- **Hydrate deliberately.** A glass of water with each drink and another before bed is a reasonable habit.
- **Watch for muscle cramps or weakness.** Thiazides can lower sodium and potassium, and vomiting or diarrhea after drinking can lower them further. (Losartan pushes potassium the other way, so in the combination pill the effects partly offset each other, but heavy fluid losses can still throw things off.)
- **Gout.** Thiazides can raise uric acid, and beer and spirits also raise uric acid. People on hydrochlorothiazide who are prone to gout may find heavy drinking sets off flares.
- **Sun.** Hydrochlorothiazide can make your skin more sun-sensitive. Day drinking outdoors in summer adds sunburn and dehydration to the list.

## Losartan and Alcohol Side Effects: What You Might Notice

These are the effects people most commonly report when they drink while taking losartan. Most are mild and pass as the alcohol wears off.

- **Dizziness or light-headedness**, especially when standing up. This is the most common one.
- **Feeling faint or actually fainting.** Less common, more serious, and more likely with dehydration, heat, or a water pill.
- **Tiredness or unusual weakness.**
- **A faster heartbeat**, as your body tries to make up for the drop in blood pressure. Alcohol on its own can also cause a racing heart; see our guide on [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) for the other causes.
- **Worse hangover dehydration** (thirst, dark urine, headache), particularly on losartan-HCTZ.
- **Falls**, which are the real-world harm that matters most, especially in older adults.

Symptoms that are **not** typical and need medical attention are listed in the next section.

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call 911 (or your local emergency number) or go to an emergency department if you have any of these after drinking on losartan:

- You **fainted**, or you nearly fainted and still feel very weak or confused.
- **Chest pain**, pressure, or tightness.
- A heartbeat that is **very slow, very irregular, or pounding** and doesn't settle.
- **Severe muscle weakness**, numbness, or tingling, which can be a sign of a dangerous potassium level.
- **Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat**, or trouble breathing or swallowing. Losartan can rarely cause this kind of swelling (angioedema), and it's an emergency whether or not you've been drinking.
- **Little or no urine for many hours** despite drinking fluids, or confusion with extreme thirst.

Call your doctor or pharmacist the same day if:

- You've had **vomiting or diarrhea** after drinking and can't keep fluids down. Ask whether to pause losartan (and any water pill) until you're eating and drinking normally.
- You keep getting **dizzy spells** after small amounts of alcohol.
- You hit your head in a fall, even if you feel fine.

If you check your own blood pressure at home, a reading that is much lower than your usual, together with symptoms like dizziness or fainting, is worth a call. A low number with no symptoms is less concerning, but it's still useful to mention at your next visit.

## Hangover Painkillers on Losartan: What to Take and What to Avoid

This is one of the most practical questions people on losartan have, and the answer isn't obvious.

**Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), and high-dose aspirin** are NSAIDs. In people taking losartan, NSAIDs can make the blood pressure medicine less effective and can strain the kidneys, especially when you're dehydrated. Add a diuretic and you get what pharmacists call the **"triple whammy"**: an ARB or ACE inhibitor, a diuretic, and an NSAID together, a combination that's known to raise the risk of acute kidney injury. A dehydrated morning after drinking is the worst possible time for it. Our [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) guide covers the stomach-bleeding risk NSAIDs carry on top of that.

**Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** doesn't affect blood pressure or kidney function the way NSAIDs do, so it's usually the pain reliever doctors prefer for people on blood pressure medicines. It has its own alcohol issue, which is the liver. A single standard dose the morning after a few drinks is generally reasonable for people who don't drink heavily day to day, but if you have three or more drinks most days, ask a doctor first. Our [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) guide explains how to use it safely.

**Low-dose aspirin** taken daily for heart protection is a separate matter. Don't stop or change it because of a hangover; ask your doctor if you have questions.

The safest hangover "treatment" for someone on losartan is mostly non-drug: water, an electrolyte drink, food, and sleep.

## Potassium, Coconut Water, and Salt Substitutes

Losartan tends to nudge potassium levels up, because blocking angiotensin II reduces aldosterone, the hormone that tells your kidneys to get rid of potassium. For most people with normal kidneys this is a small change that only shows up on blood tests. It matters more if you have kidney disease, diabetes, or take other potassium-raising medicines such as spironolactone.

That's relevant to hangover habits, because several popular hangover remedies are high in potassium:

- **Coconut water** is very high in potassium. One serving is fine for most people on losartan, but drinking large amounts every morning isn't a great idea if your potassium has ever been flagged as high. See our guide to [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover).
- **"Lite" or potassium-based salt substitutes** (often sold as low-sodium salt) can contain a lot of potassium. The losartan label cautions against them unless your doctor approves.
- **Potassium supplements** and some electrolyte powders. Check the label.

Bananas, potatoes, and other ordinary foods are generally fine as part of a normal diet. The concern is with concentrated sources and supplements, and mainly for people with reduced kidney function.

## Does Alcohol Make Losartan Less Effective?

Not in the sense of blocking the drug. Alcohol doesn't stop losartan from attaching to its receptors, and there's no good evidence that a moderate amount changes how your body absorbs or breaks down losartan in any meaningful way.

But regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure on its own, through effects on the nervous system, stress hormones, and blood vessel walls. So the overall effect can look like the medicine is "not working." If you're drinking heavily most days and your blood pressure readings are still high on losartan, the alcohol is a likely part of the reason, and cutting back is one of the most effective changes you can make. That's often a better first step than adding more medicine, and it's a conversation worth having with your doctor.

There's also an adherence effect. People who drink heavily are more likely to miss doses, take them late, or double up after forgetting, and all of those make blood pressure control worse.

## What About Other ARBs?

The same principles apply to the rest of the ARB family, because the interaction is about the shared way these medicines work, not something unique to losartan. That includes **valsartan (Diovan), irbesartan (Avapro), olmesartan (Benicar), candesartan (Atacand), and telmisartan (Micardis)**, as well as combination pills that add a diuretic (names ending in "HCT") or amlodipine.

**ACE inhibitors** such as lisinopril, enalapril, and ramipril act on the same hormone system one step earlier, and the alcohol advice for them is very similar: watch for dizziness, avoid dehydration, be careful with NSAIDs, and keep drinking moderate.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

To pull the earlier sections together, the people for whom drinking on losartan deserves a real conversation with a doctor are:

- **Anyone taking losartan-HCTZ** or another water pill alongside it.
- **People with chronic kidney disease**, including diabetic kidney disease.
- **People with heart failure**, where fluid and salt balance are already delicate.
- **Older adults** and anyone with a history of falls or fainting.
- **People on several blood pressure medicines** at once.
- **Anyone who is pregnant or could become pregnant.** Losartan carries a boxed warning against use in pregnancy because it can harm the developing baby, and alcohol in pregnancy carries its own risks. If you're pregnant or planning to be, talk to your doctor about both right away.
- **People who drink heavily on a regular basis**, both for blood pressure control and because stopping suddenly after long, heavy daily drinking can cause withdrawal, which itself can spike blood pressure and heart rate. If that applies to you, tell your doctor before cutting back so they can help you do it safely.

## Practical Tips for a Night Out on Losartan

If you've decided to drink, these habits lower your chances of trouble:

1. **Take your losartan as usual.** Don't skip it and don't double it.
2. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows alcohol absorption and softens the blood pressure dip.
3. **Pace yourself.** One drink an hour at most, and set a limit before you start.
4. **Alternate with water.** Especially if you're on losartan-HCTZ or it's hot.
5. **Stand up slowly.** Sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before getting up at night. Hold on to something.
6. **Skip the sauna, hot tub, or long hot shower** after drinking. Heat widens blood vessels too.
7. **Have a plan for the morning.** Water, food, and acetaminophen in a sensible dose if you need it, rather than ibuprofen or naproxen.
8. **If you're vomiting or have diarrhea**, call your doctor or pharmacist about pausing your dose until you can keep fluids down.

For more general ways to make the morning after easier, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people who drink occasionally use supplements to help with the morning after. The one we cover most is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on the brain's response to alcohol. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It's promising, not proven.

Two points matter for anyone on losartan:

- **DHM does nothing for the blood pressure interaction.** It won't stop alcohol from adding to losartan's effect, it won't prevent dizziness on standing, and it doesn't make it safe to drink more. There is no good evidence that DHM changes how alcohol and losartan interact in either direction.
- **There's little research on DHM alongside blood pressure medicines.** Before adding any supplement, including DHM, run it by your pharmacist. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) goes through what is and isn't known.

If your doctor is comfortable with it and you want to try DHM for occasional moderate drinking, a widely used option is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), and a lower-cost single-ingredient choice is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. None of them replaces the basics above: drink moderately, eat, hydrate, and stand up slowly.

## The Bottom Line

Losartan and alcohol don't react with each other chemically, and an occasional drink is usually fine for people on a stable dose with healthy kidneys. The risk is additive: both lower blood pressure, so together they can make you dizzy or faint, mostly when you stand up, and alcohol's dehydrating effect can strain your kidneys while losartan is blocking one of their backup systems. The combination pill with hydrochlorothiazide carries a specific alcohol warning on its label. Over the long run, heavy drinking raises blood pressure and works against your medicine. Keep drinking moderate, take your dose as usual, avoid NSAIDs for hangover pain, call your doctor if you're vomiting and can't keep fluids down, and talk to your doctor or pharmacist about what's right for you.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking losartan?**

For most people on a stable dose with healthy kidneys, light to moderate drinking (up to one drink a day for women and two for men) is generally considered acceptable. Both alcohol and losartan lower blood pressure, so the combination can cause dizziness or fainting, especially when you stand up. Ask your doctor first if you also take a water pill, have kidney disease or heart failure, or have had dizzy spells on losartan.

**How long after taking losartan can I drink alcohol?**

There isn't a meaningful waiting period. Losartan is designed to lower blood pressure around the clock, so spacing a drink a few hours from your pill won't change much. Take your dose at the usual time, don't skip it to drink, and be especially careful getting up during the night after drinking. If you've just started losartan or had your dose raised, it's sensible to hold off on alcohol until you know how it affects you.

**Is it safe to drink alcohol with losartan-HCTZ (Hyzaar)?**

It needs more care than losartan alone. The hydrochlorothiazide in the combination pill is a water pill, and its label warns that alcohol can make dizziness on standing (orthostatic hypotension) worse. Alcohol also makes you pee more, so dehydration is more likely. If you drink, keep it light, alternate with water, stand up slowly, and ask your doctor what's reasonable for you.

**What are the side effects of mixing losartan and alcohol?**

The most common effect is dizziness or light-headedness, especially when standing up. Others include tiredness, a faster heartbeat, feeling faint, and worse next-day dehydration. Fainting, chest pain, a very irregular heartbeat, severe muscle weakness, or swelling of the face, lips, or throat need emergency care right away.

**Does alcohol make losartan less effective?**

Alcohol doesn't block losartan directly, and there's no good evidence that moderate drinking changes how the drug is absorbed or broken down. But regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure on its own, so it can work against your medicine and make it look like losartan isn't working. Cutting back on heavy drinking is one of the most effective ways to improve blood pressure control.

**Can I take ibuprofen for a hangover if I'm on losartan?**

Check with your pharmacist first. Ibuprofen, naproxen, and other NSAIDs can make losartan less effective and can strain the kidneys, especially when you're dehydrated after drinking. The risk is higher if you also take a water pill. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) in a sensible single dose is usually the preferred pain reliever for people on blood pressure medicines, as long as you don't drink heavily on a regular basis.

**Should I skip my losartan dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Skipping a dose can let your blood pressure climb, and it doesn't make drinking meaningfully safer because losartan's effect carries over. Take it as usual and drink moderately. The one exception is if you're vomiting or have diarrhea and can't keep fluids down. In that case, call your doctor or pharmacist about pausing it until you're eating and drinking normally again.

**Does DHM help if I drink while taking losartan?**

There is no good evidence that DHM changes the interaction between alcohol and losartan. It won't prevent the blood pressure drop or dizziness, and it doesn't make it safe to drink more. There's also little research on DHM alongside blood pressure medicines, so check with your pharmacist before adding it.
